en: A devoted follower or assistant
hook: ACOLYTE: A COLLEAGUE who follows you everywhere like a shadow.
story: Acolyte. Professor Rahman is famous for his theory of river erosion. Wherever he lectures, a small band of former students follows him: they carry his slides, quote his books word for word, and defend him fiercely online. Critics call them his acolytes: devoted followers or assistants. Originally an acolyte was an altar assistant in a church, lighting candles for the priest. Today the word often hints at uncritical devotion. Synonyms: disciple, follower, adherent. Opposite: critic.

gre.s: Critics dismissed the young scholar as little more than the famous theorist's ____, since she repeated his ideas without ever questioning them.
gre.clue: repeated his ideas without ever questioning them

en: To choose someone ceremonially for a role; to apply oil as part of a religious ceremony
bn: অভিষিক্ত করা; উত্তরাধিকারী হিসেবে মনোনীত করা
hook: ANOINT: kings were 'A-OIL-ed' — oil on the head at coronation.
story: Anoint. When the old headmaster of a famous Dhaka school announced his retirement, everyone wondered who would replace him. At the farewell assembly, he called young Mr. Imran to the stage, placed his own fountain pen in his hand, and declared him the next headmaster. He had anointed his successor: chosen him ceremonially for the role. Literally, to anoint is to rub with holy oil, as kings were anointed at coronations. Today the media anoint rising stars and front-runners.

gre.s: Although many party insiders expected an open contest, the retiring leader chose to ____ his deputy as successor, effectively ending the race before it began.
gre.clue: effectively ending the race before it began

en: Morally low; without principles or dignity
hook: GRE trick: BASE means LOW morally, like the bottom of a building.
story: Base. During a flood, a shopkeeper in Sunamganj hoarded rice and sold it to hungry families at three times the normal price. When a relief volunteer pleaded with him, he laughed and raised the price again. The villagers called his behaviour base: morally low, without principles or dignity. This base has nothing to do with a foundation. Think of debased, meaning lowered in value. Base motives include greed, cowardice, and spite. Synonyms: ignoble, vile, contemptible. Opposite: noble.

gre.s: Investigators concluded that the official had acted from the most ____ motives, since he had accepted bribes to approve a dam he knew was unsafe.
gre.clue: accepted bribes to approve a dam he knew was unsafe

en: The use of force or threats to make someone do something
hook: COERCION: COERCE = FORCE.
story: Coercion. A garment worker in Gazipur was told by her supervisor that unless she signed a form giving up her overtime pay, she would lose her job. She signed, in tears. Later, a labour court ruled the signature worthless because it was obtained through coercion: the use of force or threats to make someone do something. The verb is coerce. A confession made under coercion is not voluntary. Synonyms: compulsion, intimidation, duress. Opposite: free consent.

gre.s: The court threw out the confession, ruling that it had been obtained not through voluntary cooperation but through ____, since the suspect had been threatened with violence.
gre.clue: the suspect had been threatened with violence

en: To invent a new word or phrase
hook: GRE trick: to COIN a word is to MINT a brand-new one, like a new coin.
story: Coin. Tasnim's little brother invented a word for the panic students feel the night before exam results: resultitis. Within a month, the whole hostel was using it. He had coined a new word: invented it. Writers and scientists coin terms all the time. Shakespeare is credited with coining hundreds of words, and selfie was coined only recently. Picture a mint stamping out shiny new coins: coining a phrase stamps out something new. Synonyms: invent, devise, originate.

gre.s: Rather than borrow an existing term, the psychologist decided to ____ a new one, since no word in the language captured the phenomenon she had discovered.
gre.clue: no word in the language captured the phenomenon

en: Clever at achieving goals through deceit or skill
hook: CUNNING: as clever as a fox.
story: Cunning. In Bengali folk tales, Shiyal Pandit, the jackal scholar, is the great trickster. In one story, a crocodile hands him her seven babies to teach. Each day the jackal eats one, and whenever the mother visits, he holds up the same baby again and again, and she never notices. The jackal is cunning: clever at reaching his goals through deceit or skill. As a noun, cunning is that sly cleverness itself. Synonyms: crafty, wily, guileful. Opposite: ingenuous.

gre.s: The diplomat was admired less for her eloquence than for her ____: she repeatedly outmaneuvered rivals by letting them believe they had already won.
gre.clue: outmaneuvered rivals by letting them believe they had already won

en: To make someone uneasy, confused, or embarrassed
hook: DIS-COMFIT: takes away your COMFORT.
story: Discomfit. Arif had prepared perfectly for his viva on rural banking. Then the external examiner asked a simple question about his own data that he had never considered. Arif's face went hot, he shuffled his papers, and he stammered for a full minute. The question had discomfited him: made him uneasy, confused, and embarrassed. Discomfit sounds like discomfort, and today the meanings are close. Originally it meant to defeat in battle. Synonyms: disconcert, fluster, unsettle. Opposite: reassure.

gre.s: The seasoned politician usually remained composed under fire, yet the student's pointed question about his voting record seemed to ____ him, and he stammered through his reply.
gre.clue: he stammered through his reply

en: To disagree with an official or widely held opinion
hook: DIS-SENT: DIS-agree with the SENTiment.
story: Dissent. At the faculty meeting, every professor voted to raise the pass mark except one. Doctor Nusrat stood up and warned that the new rule would push poor rural students out of the university. She was outvoted twenty to one, but she put her dissent on record. Dissent is disagreement with an official or majority view; to dissent is to disagree openly. A judge who disagrees with the majority writes a dissenting opinion. Opposite: assent, which means agreement.

gre.s: Although most of the committee endorsed the proposal enthusiastically, two members chose to ____, arguing that its costs had been badly underestimated.
gre.clue: arguing that its costs had been badly underestimated

en: To extract the essential meaning; to purify a liquid by heating
hook: DISTILL: boil it down to the pure essence.
story: Distill. Mahin's thesis supervisor gave him a challenge: explain your two hundred pages of research in a single sentence. Mahin spent a whole evening cutting, rewriting, and cutting again, until only the core idea remained. He had distilled it: extracted its essential meaning. Literally, to distill is to purify a liquid by heating it into vapour and cooling it back down, the way distilled water is made. In both senses, you remove everything except the essence.

gre.s: In just a few pages, the author manages to ____ decades of complex research into a handful of clear principles that any reader can grasp.
gre.clue: into a handful of clear principles

en: Doubtful; of questionable value or honesty
hook: DUBIOUS: full of DOUBT.
story: Dubious. A message arrived on Kamal's phone: he had won a brand new car in a lottery he had never entered, and only needed to send five thousand taka to claim it. The number was foreign and the spelling was terrible. Kamal was dubious, and rightly so. Dubious means doubtful, or of questionable value or honesty. A person can feel dubious about a claim, and a claim itself can be dubious. Think: dubious begins like doubt. Synonyms: suspect, questionable, shady.

gre.s: The study's conclusions are ____ at best: its sample was tiny, its funding came from the very company whose product it praised, and no one has replicated it.
gre.clue: its funding came from the very company whose product it praised

en: Cheerful and full of energy; bubbling with enthusiasm
hook: EBULLIENT: BUBBLING over like boiling water.
story: Ebullient. Mehjabin had been rejected by five universities. Then one morning an email arrived: a full scholarship to study in Canada. She ran through the hostel shouting, hugged the cook, called her mother, and danced on the roof. For the rest of the week she was ebullient: cheerful, full of energy, bubbling over with enthusiasm. Ebullient literally means boiling up, from Latin bullire, to boil. Picture happiness bubbling over a pot. Synonyms: exuberant, buoyant, effervescent. Opposite: morose.

gre.s: Normally reserved and soft-spoken, the professor was uncharacteristically ____ at the reception, laughing loudly and greeting every guest with a warm embrace.
gre.clue: laughing loudly and greeting every guest with a warm embrace

en: Treating serious issues with inappropriate humor
hook: FACETIOUS: makes funny FACES at serious things.
story: Facetious. At a serious meeting about rising dropout rates, the principal asked for ideas. Zubair raised his hand and suggested they simply cancel exams, so that nobody could ever fail. A few teachers smiled; the principal did not. His remark was facetious: treating a serious issue with inappropriate humor. Facetious is joking at the wrong moment. A handy trick: facetious contains all five vowels, a, e, i, o, u, in order, as neat as a joke. Synonyms: flippant, glib, tongue-in-cheek.

gre.s: The minister's ____ remark about the flood victims, which he apparently intended as a joke, provoked outrage among families who had lost everything.
gre.clue: which he apparently intended as a joke

en: Capable of making mistakes
hook: FALLIBLE: able to FALL into error.
story: Fallible. Doctor Ahmed had practised medicine for thirty years. When a junior doctor questioned his diagnosis, he listened, ordered another test, and discovered he had been wrong. He thanked her. "Experience makes you better, but never perfect. Every doctor is fallible." Fallible means capable of making mistakes. It shares a root with fail and false. Its opposite, infallible, means incapable of error. Human memory is notoriously fallible. Synonyms: imperfect, error-prone, unreliable.

gre.s: Eyewitness testimony, once treated as nearly conclusive, is now known to be highly ____, since memories can be distorted by stress, suggestion, and the passage of time.
gre.clue: memories can be distorted by stress, suggestion, and the passage of time

en: Excessively elaborate or ornate; having a red or flushed complexion
hook: FLORID: covered in FLOWERS, too decorated.
story: Florid. Tanvir's cousin wrote his own wedding invitation. Instead of saying please come, it read: "Upon this most auspicious and radiant evening, when the very moon bows in jubilation, your gracious and illustrious presence is humbly beseeched." Everyone laughed. The style was florid: excessively elaborate or ornate. Florid comes from Latin flos, flower; think of prose with too many flowers. Florid can also describe a flushed, red face. Synonyms: ornate, flowery, overwrought. Opposite: austere.

gre.s: Readers accustomed to the novelist's spare, unadorned prose were startled by the ____ style of her latest book, crowded with elaborate metaphors and lush adjectives.
gre.clue: crowded with elaborate metaphors and lush adjectives

en: Awkward and clumsy, often because tall and thin
hook: GAWKY: like a young GOOSE that hasn't learned to walk.
story: Gawky. At fourteen, Ayon grew fifteen centimetres in a single year. Suddenly his arms seemed too long for his sleeves, he knocked over glasses at dinner, and he tripped over his own feet on the football field. His aunties teased him lovingly. He was gawky: awkward and clumsy, especially because tall and thin. Picture a young giraffe learning to walk. Gawky teenagers often grow into graceful adults. Synonyms: ungainly, gangling, lanky. Opposite: graceful.

gre.s: The once ____ teenager, who used to trip over his own feet, had grown into a dancer of remarkable poise and elegance.
gre.clue: who used to trip over his own feet

en: To persuade someone by flattery or deception
hook: INVEIGLE: like a VEIL over the truth to lure someone in.
story: Inveigle. A smooth-talking salesman visited Rahim's grandfather in Cumilla. He praised the old man's wisdom, admired his garden, called him uncle, and touched his feet. Within an hour, he had talked him into signing up for an expensive insurance plan he did not need. The salesman had inveigled him: persuaded him by flattery or deception. Hear the word as in-vague-le: luring someone in with vague, sweet talk. Synonyms: cajole, wheedle, entice, beguile.

gre.s: Through a combination of flattery and false promises, the con artist managed to ____ several elderly investors into handing over their life savings.
gre.clue: Through a combination of flattery and false promises

en: To throw away or abandon something unwanted
hook: JETTISON: a JET dumping fuel to lighten its load.
story: Jettison. Halfway up the steep road to Sajek, the overloaded jeep began to stall. The driver ordered everyone out and made them throw away the heavy extras: a crate of soft drinks, two broken plastic chairs, and an old speaker. The lighter jeep climbed easily. They had jettisoned the extra weight. To jettison is to throw away or abandon something unwanted. Sailors once jettisoned cargo to save sinking ships. Companies jettison failing plans. Synonyms: discard, abandon, scrap.

gre.s: Faced with mounting losses, the company decided to ____ its least profitable divisions so that it could focus its resources on its core business.
gre.clue: so that it could focus its resources on its core business

en: Untruthfulness; the habit of lying
hook: MENDACITY: MEN DARE lie.
story: Mendacity. A local politician promised a new bridge, then claimed it had been built, then claimed the river had changed course, then blamed the villagers for the delay. Every week brought a new lie. Eventually even his supporters stopped believing anything he said. They were tired of his mendacity: his untruthfulness, his habit of lying. Do not confuse mendacity, lying, with mendicancy, begging. The adjective is mendacious. Synonyms: dishonesty, deceit, duplicity. Opposite: veracity.

gre.s: The memoir was celebrated as a model of candor until journalists exposed its author's ____: many of its most moving episodes had simply been invented.
gre.clue: many of its most moving episodes had simply been invented

en: Very generous
hook: MUNIFICENT: MONEY-FICENT, gives money generously.
story: Munificent. When the village school in Beanibazar was about to close for lack of money, a former pupil who had become a successful restaurant owner in London heard the news. He paid for a new building, a library, a computer lab, and scholarships for fifty children every year. The village called him munificent: very generous. Munificent suggests giving on a grand scale. Think: munificent gifts are magnificent gifts. Synonyms: bountiful, lavish, generous. Opposite: miserly, parsimonious.

gre.s: Far from being the miser his neighbors believed him to be, the reclusive farmer proved ____, leaving his entire fortune to the village school.
gre.clue: leaving his entire fortune to the village school

en: Showing a lack of experience, wisdom, or judgment
hook: NAIVE: like a NATIVE newcomer who doesn't know the city's tricks.
story: Naive. On her first day in Dhaka, Ruma believed every rickshaw puller who said his fare was fixed, gave her phone number to a stranger promising a cheap flat, and paid for a genuine gold chain at a roadside stall. Her city cousins laughed. She was naive: showing a lack of experience, wisdom, or judgment. Naive comes from the same root as native, meaning born; a naive person is like a newborn in the world. Synonyms: credulous, gullible, ingenuous. Opposite: worldly.

gre.s: Only a ____ observer would take the company's promises at face value, since it has broken nearly every pledge it has made in the past decade.
gre.clue: since it has broken nearly every pledge it has made in the past decade

en: Having high moral qualities; aristocratic
hook: NOBLE: like a NOBEL Prize-worthy character.
story: Noble. A rickshaw puller in Dhaka found a bag containing two lakh taka under his seat. He was poor, and his daughter needed school fees. Still, he spent the whole day searching until he found the owner, returned every note, and refused any reward. The newspapers called his act noble: showing high moral qualities. Noble also means aristocratic, as in a noble family, but the GRE usually wants the moral sense. Synonyms: honourable, virtuous, magnanimous. Opposite: base.

gre.s: Although she could easily have kept the reward for herself, she made the ____ choice to donate it to the families of the miners who had died.
gre.clue: Although she could easily have kept the reward for herself

en: Having a limited or narrow outlook
hook: PAROCHIAL: limited to the local PARISH.
story: Parochial. Uncle Habib has lived his whole life in one neighbourhood of Old Dhaka. He believes the best biryani, the best tailors, and the best people are all within three streets of his house, and he dismisses any idea from outside as foolish. His views are parochial: limited and narrow in outlook. The word comes from parish, a small church district; a parochial mind never leaves its own parish. Synonyms: provincial, insular, narrow-minded. Opposite: cosmopolitan.

gre.s: Critics complained that the festival had become increasingly ____, showcasing only local filmmakers and ignoring the vibrant international cinema it had once championed.
gre.clue: showcasing only local filmmakers and ignoring the vibrant international cinema

en: Lacking inspiration or excitement; dull
hook: GRE trick: PEDESTRIAN = as dull as plodding along on foot.
story: Pedestrian. Sumaiya read the winning essay from a national competition and frowned. The grammar was perfect, but every idea was predictable, every example borrowed, every sentence safe. Nothing surprised her. She called it pedestrian: lacking inspiration or excitement, dull and ordinary. Yes, it is the same word as a person walking on foot. Think of writing that plods along at walking pace and never takes flight. Synonyms: mundane, prosaic, uninspired, humdrum. Opposite: imaginative.

gre.s: Although the film's special effects were dazzling, its plot was disappointingly ____, recycling clichés that audiences had seen countless times before.
gre.clue: recycling clichés that audiences had seen countless times before

en: To speak or act evasively to avoid the truth
bn: সত্য এড়িয়ে যাওয়া; ঘুরিয়ে কথা বলা
hook: PREVARICATE: PRE-VARY the truth, twist it.
story: Prevaricate. Nayeem's mother asked him directly whether he had gone to his coaching class that day. He talked about the traffic, the heat, a friend who was sick, and how the teacher sometimes cancels classes. He never actually said yes or no. His mother sighed. He was prevaricating: speaking evasively to avoid the truth. Prevaricate comes from a Latin word for walking crookedly. Do not confuse it with procrastinate, which means to delay. Synonyms: equivocate, hedge, dodge.

gre.s: Pressed repeatedly about the missing funds, the treasurer continued to ____, offering vague answers that neither admitted nor denied any wrongdoing.
gre.clue: offering vague answers that neither admitted nor denied any wrongdoing

en: To prepare someone or something for action
hook: GRE trick: to PRIME is to PREPARE, like priming a wall before painting.
story: Prime. In the week before Mitu's GRE, her tutor taught her nothing new. Instead, he gave her timed practice sets every morning at the exact hour of the real test, so her brain would be ready to focus at that time. He was priming her: preparing her for action. Painters prime a wall with a base coat before the real colour. Old water pumps must be primed before they work. Synonyms: prepare, ready, groom. Opposite: neglect.

gre.s: Before the negotiations began, the lawyer took care to ____ her client, rehearsing every likely question so that nothing would catch him off guard.
gre.clue: rehearsing every likely question so that nothing would catch him off guard

en: Favoring drastic change; relating to the fundamental nature of something
hook: RADICAL: down to the ROOT (radix).
story: Radical. For years, a village in Kurigram tried small fixes against flooding: higher plinths, sandbags, better drains. Nothing worked. Then a young engineer proposed something radical: rebuild the whole village on floating platforms that rise with the water. Radical means favouring drastic change, or relating to the fundamental nature of something. It comes from Latin radix, root, as in radish; radical change goes all the way to the roots. Synonyms: drastic, sweeping, fundamental. Opposite: incremental.

gre.s: Rather than tinkering with the existing curriculum, the new principal proposed a ____ overhaul that would reshape every course from the ground up.
gre.clue: reshape every course from the ground up

en: Breaking out again after a period of inactivity
hook: RE-CRUDE-SCENT: the crude problem RE-emerges.
story: Recrudescent. For years, people in one hill district believed malaria had been beaten. Then, after an unusually wet season, cases suddenly began appearing again in village after village. Health officers warned of recrudescent malaria: breaking out again after a period of inactivity. The noun is recrudescence. Re means again, and crude comes from Latin crudus, raw, like a wound turning raw once more. Recrudescent violence follows the same pattern. Synonyms: resurgent, recurring, reawakened. Opposite: dormant.

gre.s: Just when historians had declared the old nationalist rivalries extinct, a ____ wave of ethnic hostility swept the region, reviving conflicts dormant for half a century.
gre.clue: reviving conflicts dormant for half a century

en: Relating to worldly as opposed to spiritual matters; relating to time
hook: TEMPORAL: TEMPORARY earthly things versus eternal spiritual ones.
story: Temporal. The old imam in Tania's village never spoke about politics, land disputes, or money from the pulpit. "My concern is the soul," he said. "Temporal matters belong to the courts and the union council." Temporal means relating to worldly life, as opposed to spiritual matters. It can also mean relating to time, as in the temporal order of events. Think of tempo and temporary; worldly things last only for a time. Opposites: spiritual, eternal.

gre.s: The medieval church claimed authority not only over spiritual life but also over ____ affairs, collecting taxes and settling property disputes like any secular ruler.
gre.clue: collecting taxes and settling property disputes like any secular ruler

en: Not permanent; lasting a short time
hook: TRANSITORY: in TRANSIT, passing through.
story: Transitory. On Pohela Boishakh, Dhaka bursts with colour: giant masks, music, red and white saris, crowds filling every street. By the next morning, the decorations are gone and the city is back to its usual traffic. Rumana thought about how transitory the joy was: lasting only a short time. Transitory is related to transit and transition, words about passing through. Fame, youth, and moods are often called transitory. Synonyms: fleeting, ephemeral, evanescent. Opposite: permanent.

gre.s: The economic boom proved ____: within two years, the new factories had closed and unemployment had returned to its former levels.
gre.clue: within two years, the new factories had closed

en: Capable of working successfully; feasible
hook: VIABLE: has VITALITY, can survive.
story: Viable. Sakib wanted to open a rooftop café in Dhanmondi. Before investing his savings, he studied the rent, counted the people passing by each evening, priced the coffee, and estimated how many customers he needed each day. The numbers worked. The plan was viable: capable of working successfully, feasible. Viable comes from French vie, life; a viable seed can live and grow. Synonyms: feasible, workable, practicable. Opposite: unworkable.

gre.s: Although solar power was once dismissed as too expensive, falling costs have made it a ____ alternative to coal in many countries.
gre.clue: falling costs have made it
